content: 1. Metoprolol has been confirmed to exhibit beta-1 selectivity. In normal subjects, it does not reverse the beta-2-mediated vasodilatory effects of epinephrine, unlike nonselective beta-blockers, which completely reverse these effects. 2. In asthmatic patients, metoprolol causes significantly less reduction in FEV1 and FVC compared to propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, when administered at equivalent beta-1 receptor-blocking doses. 3. The relationship between plasma metoprolol levels and the reduction in exercise heart rate is independent of the pharmaceutical formulation. Using an Emax model, the maximum effect observed is a 30% reduction in exercise heart rate, attributed to beta-1 blockade. 4. Beta-1 blocking effects, ranging from 30% to 80% of the maximal effect (approximately 8% to 23% reduction in exercise heart rate), correspond to plasma metoprolol concentrations between 30 and 540 nmol/L. 5. At plasma concentrations above 300 nmol/L, the relative beta-1 selectivity of metoprolol diminishes, and beta-2 adrenergic receptor blockade increases. 6. While beta-adrenergic receptor blockade is beneficial in treating angina, hypertension, and heart failure, there are situations where sympathetic stimulation is critical. For example, in patients with severely damaged hearts, adequate ventricular function may rely on sympathetic drive. 7. In the presence of AV block, beta-blockade may inhibit the necessary facilitation of conduction by sympathetic activity. 8. Beta-2 adrenergic blockade can lead to passive bronchial constriction by interfering with endogenous adrenergic bronchodilator activity in patients prone to bronchospasm. It may also interfere with the action of exogenous bronchodilators in such patients. 9. Treatment with Toprol XL has been shown to improve left ventricular ejection fraction and delay the increase in left ventricular end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes after six months of therapy. 10. In adults, metoprolol is rapidly and completely absorbed. However, following oral administration of conventional metoprolol tablets, plasma levels are approximately 50% of those achieved with intravenous administration, indicating about 50% first-pass metabolism. 11. Metoprolol crosses the blood-brain barrier and has been detected in cerebrospinal fluid at concentrations approximately 78% of simultaneous plasma levels. 12. Plasma levels of metoprolol after oral administration are highly variable, and only a small fraction (about 12%) of the drug is bound to human serum albumin. 13. Metoprolol is a racemic mixture of Rand S-enantiomers and is primarily metabolized by the enzyme CYP2D6. Its metabolism is stereoselective and dependent on oxidation phenotype. 14. Elimination of metoprolol occurs mainly through biotransformation in the liver, with a plasma half-life ranging from approximately 3 to 7 hours. Less than 5% of an oral dose is excreted unchanged in the urine, with the remainder excreted as metabolites that lack beta-blocking activity. 15. Following intravenous administration, approximately 10% of the drug is recovered unchanged in the urine. 16. The systemic availability and half-life of metoprolol in patients with renal failure do not differ significantly from those in normal subjects. Therefore, dosage adjustments are generally not required in patients with chronic renal failure. 17. CYP2D6, the primary enzyme responsible for metoprolol metabolism, is absent in about 8% of Caucasians (poor metabolizers) and about 2% of most other populations. This enzyme can be inhibited by various drugs. 18. Poor metabolizers and extensive metabolizers who concurrently use CYP2D6-inhibiting drugs may experience significantly increased metoprolol blood levels, reducing its cardioselectivity. 19. Compared to conventional metoprolol, Toprol XL produces lower peak plasma levels, a longer time to peak, and significantly reduced peak-to-trough variation. Peak plasma levels following once-daily administration of Toprol XL are approximately one-fourth to one-half of those achieved with conventional metoprolol. 20. At steady state, the average bioavailability of metoprolol with Toprol XL, across a dosage range of 50 to 400 mg once daily, is 77% relative to corresponding doses of conventional metoprolol. However, beta-1 blockade over the 24-hour dosing interval is comparable and dose-related. 21. The bioavailability of metoprolol increases with dose in a dose-related but not directly proportional manner and is not significantly affected by food when administered as Toprol XL. 22. In pediatric hypertensive patients aged 6 to 17 years, the pharmacokinetics of Toprol XL were similar to those observed in adults. Age, gender, race, and ideal body weight had no significant effects on metoprolol pharmacokinetics. Apparent oral clearance increased linearly with body weight. 23. The pharmacokinetics of metoprolol have not been studied in patients under 6 years of age. 24. Long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of metoprolol tartrate. In 2-year studies in rats at doses up to 800 mg/kg/day, there was no increase in the development of benign or malignant neoplasms of any type. 25. In a 21-month study in Swiss albino mice at doses up to 750 mg/kg/day, benign lung tumors (small adenomas) occurred more frequently in female mice receiving the highest dose compared to untreated controls. However, there was no increase in malignant or total lung tumors, nor in the overall incidence of tumors. 26. A repeat 21-month study in CD-1 mice showed no statistically or biologically significant differences in tumor incidence between treated and control groups of either sex. 27. Genotoxicity tests on metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate, including dominant lethal studies, chromosome studies, mutagenicity tests, and nucleus anomaly tests, were negative. 28. No evidence of impaired fertility due to metoprolol tartrate was observed in rats at doses up to 22 times the daily dose of 200 mg in a 60-kg patient. 29. In five controlled studies in healthy subjects, the extent and duration of beta-1 blockade produced by Toprol XL and immediate-release metoprolol were compared. Both formulations were administered in a dose range equivalent to 100-400 mg of immediate-release metoprolol per day. 30. In these studies, Toprol XL was administered once daily, while immediate-release metoprolol was administered once to four times daily.
